The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  A modulated model incorporating the most effective augmentation strategy is then developed to create a straightforward yet precise data augmentation method that can be applied to other NLP tasks involving lexical resources.  This study's findings have been validated through a range of experiments, offering potential directions for future research presented in the process of analysis. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding was further confirmed by analyzing data sets totaling 15 inverse nanobarns of luminosity at a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy, with the cross section for top quark pairs narrowing to a 2-nanobarn uncertainty and remaining in line with theoretical predictions. The study was notable for setting multiple benchmarks, given the challenging nature of extracting the signal from abundant background noise. The data sets analyzed had the highest recorded energies for proton-lead collisions at the time of discovery. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework shows promising performance when database contents are accessible, with results showing potential for enhancing existing state-of-the-art models. All proposed approaches are evaluated and demonstrated through accessible database text-to-SQL examples. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our complex network's advantages are illustrated in simulations of the 2D Hubbard model, where we successfully overcome the sign problem and accurately determine the phase boundary separating manageable and unbearable sign problems. Furthermore, this method demonstrates substantial efficiency in determining critical temperatures, achieving a 10 times reduction in the determinant cost compared to standard re-weighting techniques. Our code is available at https://github.com/ComplexNetworkLab/SignProblems.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy. Additionally, we determine that for a given basis change matrix A, the associated map σ_A preserves or sets all currents with zero topological entropy, in addition to possessing the property of being uniquely determined by its action on the basic currents associated with the full group F_A. Lastly, we establish that the map σ_A is continuous when examining the space of currents defined by a compact space K, but it's not uniformly continuous when examining the space of currents defined by a compact space K for the standard metric, although it is so for the metric d_C. Furthermore, we find that the topological entropy of currents can change after applying a basis change, in addition to not being invariant under the action of monoid morphisms, as seen with the example of the map σ_A constructed from a shift function, which shows that combining two currents with positive topological entropy results in a current with zero topological entropy. Nevertheless, we do observe that both definitions of topological entropy coincide when examining the space of currents defined by a compact space K for the metric d_C. Moreover, we determine that the set of currents with positive topological entropy is closed under the action of free group basis changes and non-erasing monoid morphisms, in addition to being preserved under the operation of taking shifts, which allows us to identify a specific current with positive topological entropy. Finally, we establish that the property of having positive topological entropy is decidable for the currents defined by a compact space K.

In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. To validate our approach, we compared our method against alternative machine learning models and discussed the implications of our findings for future research. To facilitate replication, we made our code available online. The widespread transmission of the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical importance of managing online health anxieties and preventing the spread of related rumors, as evident from our analysis. The data and algorithms used in this study are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenghaoLi/COVID-19_Rumor_Spread. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned four-dimensional mapping of galaxies will be enhanced by applying this method to a broader range of galaxies. The methodology for calculating distances based on planetary nebulae frequency distributions will serve as a reliable standard for the evaluation of such observations. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its versatility and high-performance capabilities, LifeStream is suitable for multiple application domains, not just healthcare. The system's efficient design, coupled with its open source nature, allows users to customize LifeStream easily, enabling a wide range of stream processing tasks across various settings. The underlying technology has far-reaching potential for generalization, as evidenced by the accompanying micro-benchmark results, which demonstrate LifeStream's scalability and life cycles analysis indicating its optimal performance across different dataset characteristics. The source code of LifeStream is publicly available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/StreamML/LifeStream}.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we derive the equation that a curve must satisfy in order to be considered a timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, providing examples of curves that fit this category and those that do not. Furthermore, we establish that the Frenet frame of these curves undergoes a specific change, called the 1-3 Bertrand transformation, which serves as a natural generalization of the usual Darboux transformation. This transformation is useful in analyzing the properties of both the curve and the frame that defines it. Additionally, we find that the (1,3)-Bertrand curves are constant curvature curves, except in the two-dimensional Euclidean space where they are Bertrand curves. This exception is illustrated with an example. Moreover, we establish that the 1-3 Bertrand transformation preserves the curvature of the Frenet frame, which is a property that defines this transformation. This work also introduces the concept of closed curves and shows that not all timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves are closed curves, providing an example of a curve that is not closed. Furthermore, we derive the equation for a closed and periodic curve, and demonstrate that this equation can be simplified to the Kosambi-Curvature equation, which has a significant implication for the research community. This achievement is a natural generalization of a previous achievement that was applicable to the two-dimensional Euclidean space. This generalization provides a significant contribution to the field of differential geometry and provides a new research direction for the scientific community. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple, adaptive strategy that leads to notable improvements in specific cases. Our work is applicable to a broad range of tasks, including adaptive learning, where we achieve results comparable to state-of-the-art non-adaptive methods. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrasoul/EvalLoss.

A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. Consequently, for BPSK-Mask and MSK, the ideal delay periods are found to be 3 and 5 symbols, respectively. It is also demonstrated that for these CPM formats, the ideal delay periods coincide with those selected based on the FER error criterion. Moreover, through further analysis, it is shown that the minimum Euclidean distance criterion is equivalent to the maximum likelihood sequence estimation MLSE threshold criterion, which is based on the accumulated metric, allowing for its computation for any CPM format. This leads to a general formula for calculating the delay period $\bar{K}$ as the smallest integer value satisfying the condition $\bar{K} \geq (d_{\min}^2 \cdot \rho)/2$, where $\rho$ is the signal-to-noise ratio. This formula can be applied to any CPM format, making it a universally applicable performance evaluation metric. In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive performance evaluation of conventional differential detection using CPM signals, offering a precise analysis of its performance, as well as an implementation guide for its optimization in various applications. This research can be extended to non-coherent detection techniques based on differential detection in various communication scenarios. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC is further underscored by our investigation into the underlying principles governing this dataset, and we highlight potential pathways for related research topics.  The detailed specifications of ATOMIC, coupled with the availability of a user-friendly interactive tool that enables exploration of this dataset, is now available online.  Our proposed framework for conditioning generative models on conditional patterns resulting from ATOMIC has been successfully applied to challenging real-world tasks, and our open-sourced code can be found at https://github.com/petermu/condition-finetune.  We have also launched a related website that is accessible at https://atomic-data.org.  Our research has further implications for intricate models of artificial intelligence and we discuss these in greater detail in the comprehensive theoretical analysis presented in the appendix.  The massive scale of ATOMIC, comprising over 900,000 text-based descriptions, makes it an ideal target for modeling the complexities of everyday reasoning, and we believe that it represents a landmark achievement in the development of artificial commonsense. Ultimately, our findings have significant ramifications for the underlying principles governing everyday inferential knowledge, and we are confident that they will be a source of inspiration for the artificial intelligence research community. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. Moreover, NISQ-HHL is presently available on GitHub, coupled with an interactive portfolio optimization example.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This approach also surpasses the performance of E2E ASR models trained with masked speech reconstruction. The resulting model also demonstrates its ability to handle long text inputs by incorporating a self-attention mechanism in the decoder. The code for this project is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/speech-text-modal-training.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The conditioned random walk is analyzed using large deviation theory, and this analysis enables us to establish the asymptotic independence and distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations. The distance between the empirical distribution and the uniform distribution is quantified as an application of large deviation theory, which is the basis for our rate bounds and limit theorems. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The observed effects also prompt a re-examination of the assumption that coherent quantum phase slips are the primary obstacle to conduction in these nanowires. The role of Coulomb blockade in this context is discussed as a more plausible explanation for the data, although the issue of the gate-controlled periodic shifts remains unconcluded. The discrepancy with existing literature on the critical voltage threshold for Coulomb blockade in these nanowires is also noted. The occurrence of these period shifts during measurements suggests the presence of discrete charge configurations in the nanowires and offers potential for exploring the interplay between phase slips and Coulomb blockade. The research utilized a novel measurement setup that combined a highly sensitive dc conduction measurement system with a precise control of the gate electrode using a piezoelectric actuator, uncovering the complex relationships between voltage, capacitance, and the conduction threshold. The findings have implications for using nanowires in quantum interference devices and emphasize the necessity of considering the interplay between Coulomb blockade and phase slips in these systems. The project involved the design and construction of a custom measurement setup using a lock-in technique and a dc conduction measurement system, as well as the development of a data acquisition protocol that integrated the operation of the piezoelectric actuator with the measurement equipment, allowing for the precise tracking of the actuator's position and subsequent calculation of the associated capacitance and charge configuration. The research was conducted in the Physics Department at the Royal Military College in Kingston, Ontario, Canada. The results are published in the journal Physical Review B. The research was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the Canadian Institute for Military and Naval Technology. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhinavd1609/novel-view-prediction.

We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications. The scalability and versatility of this device concept were also highlighted. The development of a database for photonic mode profiles was also proposed, which could serve as a reference for research and industrial purposes. The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Although the model assumes a non-relativistic description of quarks, it yields results that align with the Bethe-Salpeter approach for the ground state and the intrinsic properties of the ground and first excited states of the quark systems, despite some overestimation of mass components. Generally, the results demonstrate this model's effectiveness in predicting the Ω-baryon's properties and predicts rare decay modes and electromagnetic transitions for the Ω-baryon states. A comparison with the linear 't Hooft model that uses a different approach to describe the quark system's internal dynamics is also presented. This study's findings for the linear 't Hooft model are novel and have not been reported before. A discussion on the model's assumptions, its limitations, and the potential for it to be applied to other hadron systems is also included. A comprehensive survey of existing experimental and theoretical data on the Ω-baryon's mass and magnetic moment is presented in the appendix. This study has further implications for the understanding of hadron mass structures and the magnetic moments of hadrons. A new approach to analyzing the magnetic moments of hadrons, based on the relation between the mass and magnetic moment of hadron systems, has been developed and successfully applied to the Ω-baryon. This approach predicts the magnetic moment of the likely exotic θ+ baryon and provides a method for determining the magnetic moments of other hadron systems, such as mesons and baryon mesons, and identifies a relation between the mass and magnetic moment that holds true for all hadron systems. A discussion on the possible formations of hadron systems and the characteristics of their mass and magnetic moment components is also included. A new perspective on the θ+ baryon's mass, based on this analysis, is presented along with a possible explanation for the challenges in detecting this particle and the potential for it to be identified as a state of hadron matter rather than a particle. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In considering the practical applications of these models, we also explored the conditions under which the 'well mixed' model could be a reliable proxy for its more intricate counterpart. In doing so, we determined that such a situation might occur in situations where the bus is operating at high speeds or when the ventilation system is highly efficient. In contrast, during slow movement or poor ventilation, the 'well mixed' model significantly underestimates the degree of variation in the distribution of aerosol particles. In studying the retention time of aerosol particles within the bus, we found that the 'well mixed' model tends to overestimate this time relative to the detailed model. In considering the retention time of a bus stop, we found that it can be accurately calculated using a simple exponential model. In exploring the dispersal of aerosol particles within the bus, we found that the direction of airflow has a significant impact, with a change in airflow direction resulting in a change in the dispersal of aerosol particles from parabolic to Gaussian in nature. In examining the effect of a sneeze on the dispersal of aerosol particles within the bus, we found that it can be significant, with the retention time of the particles generated by a sneeze reducing by as much as half within a short period of time. In studying the impact of different ventilation methods on the dispersal of aerosol particles within the bus, we found that the retention time of the particles generated by respiration reduces by as much as 30% within a short period of time. In considering the practical applications of these findings, we also explored the utility of a 'well mixed' model in predicting the dispersal of aerosol particles within a bus, with the results showing that such a model can be accurate in certain specific situations, but may also lead to errors in other circumstances.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This conclusion is further supported by calculations of transport parameters based on average Cobalt and Bismuth properties, which match the experimental results closely. The study of magnetic and electrical transport in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers may open up new avenues of research into the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and related phenomena. The role of interface scattering in this effect is particularly noteworthy, given that this system can be seen as a simplified model of complex interface systems involving multiple layers of different materials. The inherent ease of modifying the spin-orbit coupling in this system, by adjusting the thickness of the Cobalt layers, makes it particularly suitable for exploring novel phases that may emerge with the control of spin-orbit coupling. The material parameters extracted in this study suggest that thin film Cobalt/Bismuth systems may also be utilized as suitable candidates for experimental observations of the effects of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect on the electronic and magnetic properties of two-dimensional materials. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. The analysis indicates that the generalised Mie-type potential model offers an improved understanding of quantum systems, with physical properties such as scattering phase, energy eigenvalue, and bound state eigenfunction calculated through various dimensional analyses. The paper also discusses the role of $\alpha$ in calculating energy eigenvalue and the corresponding fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. The relation between the fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function and the Schrödinger wave function is established and analysed to provide a meaningful interpretation of the fractional derivative impact on quantum systems. The analysis of a diatomic molecule demonstrates the effectiveness of the generalised Mie-type potential model, with the outcome comparable with existing works, particularly the non-relativistic closed-shell case. The paper concludes by highlighting the significance of the generalised Mie-type potential model, with the implication that the fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function provides a superior approximation of the energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction in quantum systems. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The proposed method is comparable to alternative regularisation methods when considering the number of parameters required. The associated code has been made publicly available. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code is available at https://github.com/yongchunyang/PMNet.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The data sets used in this research included university campuses, offices, shopping malls, hotels, museums, airports, sports centers, schools, and libraries among others. The most accurate model developed, with a global mean absolute error of 2.05 meters, was then applied to an extensive dataset consisting of 21 different environments for a comprehensive validation process. The research provides a reliable open-source platform available online for individuals interested in conducting their own experiments or validating the results on their own datasets. The novel machine learning-based distance estimation model developed in this research has far-reaching potential applications in various fields beyond location estimation, including remote sensing, satellite imaging, geophysics, and genetics among others. The model's versatility in incorporating multiple input metrics, combined with its simplicity and ease of implementation, makes it an ideal solution for a wide range of complex analysis and interpretation tasks in these and other disciplines. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this work identifies important considerations for future experimental studies. Lastly, a proposed scheme for a multi-pass test facility is presented. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation and the US Department of Energy.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out that determining beta_k is hard to program, but we show it's possible for graphs that are tree-like, and further that adding edges to a tree-like graph can only increase beta_k to a certain level, or keep it the same if the edge is to one of its leaves. Additionally, we find specific sizes of the smallest identifying sets for particular types of graph structures, and also a way to compute beta_k for graphs that are made up of a small number of connected components. Lastly, we examine the change in beta_k as the size of the graph changes, and discover some relationships with well known properties of trees, such as their node counts, maximum degeneracy, and the length of their longest path. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. To make the approach more effective, future developments could focus on incorporating temporal information and better handling of intense point sources. Despite its limitations, this study demonstrates a groundbreaking way to analyze Fermi data and provides code available for public use. Additionally, the team created a sharpened all-sky map from a year's worth of observations, which can be found on the Fermi Science Portal.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We further present a practical application to route planning, demonstrating how action sequences can be employed to address issues of reciprocity in fishing management. We conclude by outlining potential future research paths including evaluating the performance of query-based solutions, developing ways to generate efficient action sequences, and examining the connection between graph structure and action sequences. We also release the source code for the proposed solutions on an open platform for public use. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings, accompanied by a newly developed D&D dataset containing conversations, intentions, and a fictional world, contribute to the advancement of both chatbots and models of a learning mind. They provide a critically needed framework for evaluating chatbots through the prism of a role-playing game, offering an alternative to intent-based conversations that incorporate a rich, dynamic educational environment. Moreover, our work offers a response to the criticism that current approaches to a theory-of-mind lack real-world testing, by applying a learning-based approach to a complex, dynamic environment that reflects many aspects of a learning mind. Lastly, our development of a D&D dataset and a related evaluation metric opens up possible applications in fields beyond the development of chatbots, including educational research and the study of collaborative learning within the context of D&D. It is our hope that this work and related resources will spark a greater interest in D&D among the artificial intelligence research community, leading to novel insights and innovative solutions facilitated by the immersive nature of the game. The data, along with the code used to train the Dungeon Master, is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/DnD-Theory-Of-Mind. The challenge posed by the G4C initiative is a long-term research challenge that exceeds the scope of a single project, and as such, it is our intention to establish the Foundations of Complex Learning from Game Environments as a ongoing research agenda. The ongoing development of the DnD Theory-Of-Mind dataset, accompanied by the development of new challenges and possible solutions, will be made publicly accessible through the project website at https://dnd-depth.github.io/. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. The statistical approach also allows for the prediction of a particular folding pathway for a given protein based on its intrinsic properties, by analyzing the topological features of knotted proteins. This approach reveals that proteins with trefoil knots fold via a specific pathway characterized by a 120-degree twist in their double-loop structure. This research provides a novel perspective on the relationship between protein knots and their folding processes, and offers a new tool for biologists studying the complex relationships between protein structures, their environments, and their folding processes. This approach can be extended to the study of proteins with knot types that are more complex, such as Steinerg knots. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, it demonstrates that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the two-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is deterministic - either it's finite or it's countably infinite. Notably, if $\omega$ is uniquely defined by its rotation vector, then the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is identified as a specific subgroup of the group of rational numbers with a specific division rule, which has been previously studied by another author. This research extends and builds upon the findings of another paper by Geiges and Hermann, as well as the results of another paper by the current author.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. These connections are drawn from the fact that the effective potential associated with the number theorem can be used to interpret the generative mechanisms of the Nambu-Goldstone bosons within the context of Lie algebra geometry. This perspective on the anomalous NG theorem may have far-reaching implications for both particle physics and mathematics. Specifically, it could influence our understanding of the fundamental principles underlying the Riemann hypothesis, given its connection to the number theorem and its physical interpretation within the context of effective potential and Lie algebra geometry. Conversely, the anomalous NG theorem itself may be related to the underlying principles of the Riemann hypothesis, potentially offering a new perspective on this renowned mathematical hypothesis. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, counterfactual data of this kind at a large scale also enables seamless extension to novel perturbation types, thereby expanding its utility to other tasks. The code for this project is now publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-algorithms/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process could lead to the creation of complex oxide heterostructures with unique properties, facilitating the reuse of expensive substrate materials and reducing production costs. The specific case of GdPtSb highlights the versatility of this approach, as it results in coexistence of different epitaxial relationships between individual grains, yet remote epitaxy itself was confirmed through theoretical modeling. Finally, this study demonstrated that precise investigation of available samples, coupled with careful consideration of growth conditions and film/substrate lattice mismatches, is necessary for understanding the epitaxial relationships in Heusler compounds grown on graphene substrates. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique can be applied in real-world applications including but not limited to text-to-image generation.  The code for the project is publicly available at https://github.com/lingyu-93/Single2Multi.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Therefore, this model cannot alone explain the source of high energy gamma-rays in the galaxy.  Nevertheless, it remains a plausible explanation for radiation in a subset of galaxies, and it also suggests that low-friction environments are responsible for generating gamma-rays.  Furthermore, this model assumes that gamma-rays are produced close to the black hole, and if they are generated farther away, then it may account for the radiation in more galaxies.  Finally, the model leads to the prediction of softer cosmic neutrino spectra than previously estimated.  Hence, the upcoming BSM and CTA telescopes, with greater sensitivity to lower energy radiation, will be capable of detecting this model's predictions in many galaxies.  Therefore, this model could be verified through the joint analysis of gamma and neutrino data found in these galaxies. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
We then utilize this information to determine the minimal number of transmission
channels needed to recover the original sequence accurately when the distance between
it and the code is equal to 2r. 
In particular cases, we find that this number can be as low as 2 more than the
number of transmission channels required for an error-correcting code based on a r-sphere. 
On the other hand, we also establish that the number of transmission channels needed
to recover the original sequence accurately is equal to 2 more than the number of
transmission channels needed for an error-correcting code based on a r-sphere 
for general Hamming distance codes.

Hamming distance and find an alternative solution to this problem that can be

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform. The discovery potential for these individual eccentric signals is predicted to be limited to binaries with total mass below 10^7 M_sun, primarily due to the sensitivity constraint imposed by PTA data analysis errors. The optimal detection strategy for such signals involves searching over a narrow range of eccentricity spaces, as well as narrow frequency bands, and we provide concrete estimates for the required search parameters based on current PTA datasets. The accuracy of PTA signals induced by these binaries is also assessed and found to be capable of being matched to several seconds, which is significantly longer than their gravitational wave emission timescale. This occurs because the PTA signal accuracy is determined by the time it takes for the binary's orbital frequency to change by the same amount as the PTA data analysis error, which is slow due to the large elliptical orbit. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Eulerian gamma process, with gamma denoting a gamma distribution, is a special case of the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we show that in a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, the ASEP speed process inherits the ergodic property of the TASEP speed process, leading to the conclusion that the ASEP speed process also converges to a uniform velocity in the stationary case. Lastly, we provide a new proof of the TASEP speed process convergence, as well as the ergodic property of the TASEP speed process, utilizing the ASEP speed process and drawing on the system's hydrodynamic behavior.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our system, built using a comprehensive set of 186 primer pairs, can store objects of up to 78KB in size and offers a data density of approximately 77 gigabytes per pound of polymerase. Our evaluation demonstrates that this storage system provides significant gains in sequencing costs and greater flexibility in data management, while still utilizing the existing capabilities of PCR storage. Our proposed design can serve as a blueprint for the development of more complex and efficient DNA-based storage systems that combine hierarchy and efficient data updates with flexibility. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghasempour/dna-storage.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/zwang96/SABRA.

This can happen within a short period of $10^8$ years, primarily based on simulated observations of galaxy interactions, combined with theoretical and observational evidence.
