Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Furthermore, satellite data reveal moderate levels of radiation at the Earth's surface, supporting the notion that this event had a significant impact on the planet. Moreover, findings demonstrate that solar neutron events cause harm to high-altitude aircraft and pose a risk to space missions involving large surfaces exposed to space. Lastly, research highlights the importance of deploying ground detectors at lower elevations to enhance the effectiveness of observations and provide more comprehensive data on these events. The novel insight gained from this discovery is particularly useful for guiding future air and space safety protocols. The observed levels of neutrinos and missing energy in the solar flare suggest that a detector at a lower elevation could detect neutron decay and other rare processes that occur as a result of high energy events, such as neutrinoless double beta decay and diamond decay. The technical feasibility of constructing such a detector has been proven through the successful development of a 10 liter pure liquid scintillator for the experiment, which also enlisted the support of industry partners. The proposed detector, named SOLAR-SCINT, will comprise of 50 liters of the same pure liquid scintillator and has the capabilities of detecting a decay rate of one per second for neutron decay. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions suggest that SOLAR-SCINT can also detect diamond decay in solar flares and that it has the potential to become the most sensitive diamond decay detector in the world. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Although primarily observational in nature, this study also included theoretical analysis of the proposed scenarios, including a 2D model of angular momentum transport and a 1D model of stellar evolution with post-main sequence phases. Furthermore, we discussed the possible relationships with other known stars that exhibit similar internal rotation patterns. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's ability to handle category information and eliminate unnecessary information was validated through a further analysis of the experimental results. The code for the MetaFEND system has been made available at https://github.com/ghaithan/MetaFEND. Moreover, the dataset used in this research has been made available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1T4s6s6s?usp=sharing. This approach can be applied to detect false information on other text-based platforms like Reddit and TikTok. This research was funded by the King Saud University through the Research Group Project RF-2020-12. The authors would like to extend their appreciation to the Deanship of Scientific Research at King Saud University for the financial support. The possibility of incorporating additional features such as user information and online articles has been discussed in the paper along with the possible challenges and solutions. This paper is focused on detecting false information on unexpected events, however, the proposed MetaFEND system can be adapted to work on expected events as well. This approach can be adapted to other classification tasks such as sentiment analysis and image classification. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research also provides bounds on the solution and the time it takes for the solution to become singular. Furthermore, for $u_{0}\in H^{3}(S)$ and given smooth and odd initial conditions, we establish that the solution will degrade at a rate of $(t+1)^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}}$ and determine the exact time $\kappa^{-1}(\alpha+1)$ for both cases where $\kappa$ equals zero and the case with weak dissipation. This is demonstrated through the construction of an invariant manifold and by establishing a priori bounds on the solution. This research paper also examines the relationship with a similar equation featuring local diffusion and presents a specific example where the solution degrades in a finite amount of time. This research has been presented at the 2020 Mathematics Conference at Harvard University.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our code is currently available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/Yiseong/Graph-Translator. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. The proposed approach can be applied to other medical treatments beyond LITT. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code for the DPCRN model is available online at github.com/lingcat/DPCRN.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. Nonetheless, a persistent and considerable error is observed in relation to the expected peak flux scaling, a problem that remains unresolved but suggests the presence of small-scale turbulence modelling is essential for properly capturing the characteristics of atmospheric convection. Nonetheless, the success of this simple two-fluid model in replicating the basic features of Rayleigh-Benard convection suggests its potential value for the development of more advanced multi-fluid convection schemes. A numerical implementation of this model as well as associated results are made freely available online for the benefit of the broader scientific community.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. An
LSTM model with a simple binary classification system was able to achieve an f1-score of
0.78 in the evaluation. This model was then applied to a large-scale dataset composed of
28 million tweets, for an f1-score of 0.81. The results are expected to contribute to the
advancement of LSTM networks and provide a stepping stone for others to establish more
advanced models using deep learning techniques for high-quality sentiment analysis on Twitter.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Specifically, we show that the generation of entanglement between two independent oscillators or the onset of synchronization between two coupled oscillators leaves a distinctive signature on their joint optical tomograms. By inspecting these patterns, one can gain insight into the level of quantum correlation, both within and between the systems, without the necessity of full state reconstruction. This approach can be applied to a wide range of systems, including both discrete and continuous variables, and proves particularly useful for implementing state reconstruction via annealing, machine learning, or other complex protocols for continuous-variable systems. The reflection of dynamic change in the entanglement of a single system in the form of optical tomograms has also been investigated. The dimensions of the phase-space grid required for optical tomogram reconstruction are generally determined heuristically, yet we demonstrate that they can be determined directly from the parameters of the dynamical model. This approach allows for the precise reconstruction of the Wigner function from optical tomograms, eliminating any error associated with heuristic grid determination. The proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of systems, including both discrete and continuous variables. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. The developed framework is particularly relevant for modeling situations that involve a system with an infinite number of degrees of freedom, as seen in field theory, where transferring from a situation with a small bond dimension to one with a large bond dimension is achieved through the introduction of a proper infrared cutoff. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. We enlist the aid of mathematical examples and graphs to illustrate our results and decoupling theory in action. Our research also yields a novel interpretation of the concept of linear decoupling. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. As an additional contribution, we introduce a challenging multi-agent navigation domain, compatible with popular RL and ML platforms. As expected, learning from scratch outperforms imitation learning, and co-learned agents consistently surpass the performance of isolated agents learning alone. Moreover, our method demonstrates flexibility when combined with imitation learning from demonstrations, enabling the incorporation of valuable expert knowledge. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, comparing the data with computer-simulated results, we saw that the energy flux required some reduction by as much as 10 percent to balance the solar plasma, which could be attributed to the inherent energy fluctuations or radiative loss from the sun, although more research is needed to fully understand this behavior. Lastly, the precise analysis of the data also revealed the importance of accurately accounting for the effects of radio wave emission and the influence of solar wind instabilities on energy flux, which we plan to explore in greater detail in a related study. The current findings contribute to our understanding of the solar wind and the inner dynamics of the sun, and they have significant implications for the balance between gravitational force and outward solar wind pressure at the solar surface. The research was conducted by a large group of scientists from many different institutions. The data analysis covered various aspects of the solar wind and involved multiple approaches to studying the energy flux, from direct observation to simulated analysis, which helped clarify the underlying solar dynamics. The results of the research have been made public and are available for use by other scientists. The data from the Parker Solar Probe have the potential to reveal many more important facts about the sun, and further study of the energy flux in the inner heliosphere is necessary to better understand the behavior of the sun and the balance between its inward gravity and the outward force of the solar wind. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The code successfully reproduced the complex patterns of beam loss and charging everywhere in the ring, as well as the distribution of corrected beam emittances. The code's capabilities were further demonstrated by successfully interpreting measurements of closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, which revealed a previously unknown component of oscillation in the beam distribution. The information gathered has been utilized to improve train filling and scheduling, leading to a 5.4% reduction in filled beam intensity due to beam loss. The results from the emittance scans were also used to update the beam dynamics model, resulting in emittance growth predictions that were significantly improved and reflected the complex patterns of beam distribution, thereby reflecting long-range beam-beam effects induced by irregularities in the ring. The technique of luminosity scanning has been enhanced, as demonstrated by completing a di-lepton scan in 2016 with adjusted scan rates that minimized loss of data due to beam blow-up, and overall has proven to be a highly effective tool for beam dynamics studies and has been continuously applied during production running, incorporating new capabilities such as the TRAIN code, more precise models, and improved data analysis, ensuring even greater scientific value in the future. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. The proposed algorithm can be applied to a wide range of real-world applications, including energy management and statistical learning, following the framework presented. The paper also delves into the optimization of multi-agent systems with differentiable objective functions and provides a smooth version of the proposed algorithm, which leads to reduced communication costs. The study concludes by examining the connection between the proposed algorithm and existing learning schemes, such as stochastic gradient descent and the decentralized optimization algorithm introduced in the paper by Li, Giannelli, and Johansson, which facilitates learning in complex systems through the allocation of different roles to different agents. The paper offers various appendices that include additional details on the analysis and algorithms discussed. The authors declare no conflict of interest in this study. The open-source code related to the paper can be accessed via GitHub, and the copyright for the code is held by the respective owners. The paper comprises 13 sections, including the introduction, the setup and problem formulation, the proposed algorithm, the convergence analysis, the bound estimation, the numerical experiments, the simulation setup, the robust optimization, the smooth algorithm, the learning theory, the decentralized optimization, the learning scheme, and the conclusion. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly suitable for large-scale simulations required by modern cosmic microwave background experiments. The tool is openly available at https://github.com/ricardogens/s4cmb. The current version of's4cmb' focuses exclusively on experiments using bolometric detectors, but the package's architecture makes it easy to expand its capabilities in the future. The package includes an interactive command-line interface as well as Python API options for user customization. The package includes instrumental systematic effects that mimic real experiments through the use of parameterised models, with components including time-variant temperature fluctuations, optical cross-talk, and azimuthally symmetric ring patterns. The package also includes tools for visualizing simulated data, calculating systematic effects' impact on cosmological parameters, and generating simulated data sets for validation tests. The code has been tested using actual data from two experiments: the POLARBEAR-2 experiment at 93 GHz and the Simultaneous Emission Observations Experiment at 150 GHz. The results show that the code accurately replicates real data based on various parameters. The code is relatively fast, capable of generating actual data amounts within a few hours on a standard laptop. The package includes possible expansions to better suit future experiments with different detector technologies. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our research highlights the importance of inherent linguistic knowledge within pre-trained language models and suggests that the task of word ordering could be a useful tool for evaluating the quality of their syntactic dependencies. Moreover, we propose approaches to enhance BART's performance in this regard, which also lead to improvements in the related task of partial tree linearization. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghruvo/bart-word-ordering.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into popular deepfake detection datasets, yielding results that outperform current benchmarks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article introduces two new problems that extend upon the original problems presented by Menger. The article also establishes an equivalence between the property of having an angle function that satisfies the paragraph criterion and the presence of a specific class of isomorphisms, known as ellipse isomorphisms. The development of ellipse isomorphisms in the context of spaces with the property of betweenness allows for the generalization of a specific type of isomorphism, known as the Cauchy-Riemann isomorphism, which typically requires the presence of a metric. The article concludes by examining the relationship between the spaces with angle functions and the structure of Euclidean spaces through the use of ellipse isomorphisms, which provides a solution to the second of the original problems posed by Menger. The article also offers a solution to the first problem by modifying the paragraph criterion to the standard criterion, which was unknown to Menger at the time. The article's development of ellipse isomorphisms and the modified paragraph criterion to the standard criterion may be of independent interest to the solving of Menger's problems. The article's development assumes the general concept of the paragraph criterion, which can be applied to spaces with the property of betweenness, without the requirement of having a metric. The article provides two specific formulas for defining the paragraph criterion in the context of Euclidean spaces, which it differentiates from the standard definition of angle function due to the presence of the norm multiplier. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, we establish a bound for the second minimum of a number field and a curve, thereby generalizing earlier results. Lastly, our work also implies an unboundedness property for successive minima, as well as an unboundedness property for the set of inequalities defined by pairs of minima, enabling us to demonstrate the divisibility of certain numbers, including certain prime powers, Kac-Murdock-Spencer sums, and ordered combinations of these, and to further extend these results to the set of inequalities defined by pairs of norms and curves. For the sake of comparison, we note that a finite characterization is known to hold for the integers defining relationships between the first $n$ minima of a number field, whereas a combinatorial classification is known to hold for the integers defining relationships between the first $n$ norms of a curve. Lastly, we provide a brief discussion on the connection between our work and the problem of determining whether there exists an infinite set of isomorphism classes of number fields for which a specific property holds, a problem that is known to have a positive answer only for fields with a finite number of degree options. A note on our paper's organization follows. The preliminary section is designed to collect basic information on orders, number fields, and curves

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of October 2021, a period during which the scheme distributed approximately $321 million to users in the form of refunds and payouts. Our examination concludes by examining the implications of Forsage for platforms hosting decentralized applications, the challenges of detecting and preventing pyramid schemes, the allure of these schemes to their victims, and the limited creative potential of their designers. Lastly, our research highlights the considerable value of transparency in the implementation of blockchain technology, a notion that becomes particularly evident when examining sensitive applications like those related to privacy. Our analysis of Forsage's code and transactions is available online at https://for-sage.github.io.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We also explored possible distances for five out of the nine confirmed globular clusters as being within a kiloparsec of each other and suggested that the galaxy's bulge contains a population of globular clusters with specific metallic contents and larger distances from Earth than previously known. We have made the research data available online.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. This new class of networks can be applied to the accurate analysis of systems exhibiting power-law behaviors, not limited to those discussed in this study. The methods used to construct and analyze these networks also provide a useful framework for conducting further research on related systems. The associated tensor network can be physically realized under a specific quantum regime, and its capability for efficient calculation can be ensured while ensuring the accuracy of the representation of power-law behaviors in data. The development of these networks may have an analogy to the concept of holographic renormalization, which could be explored in the future. The associated quantum erasure correction capacity and the associated thermal capacity of these networks as well as the associated thermal Hamiltonian truncation error have been thoroughly investigated in this study. The resulting network can be compared to the previously mentioned HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range, and its differences and similarities with that system have been examined. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepProcessMining/Experiments.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet radiative signatures in massive stellar flares, with enough power to photoionize a planetary upper atmosphere, with implications for exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. This model can be a useful tool in interpreting the effects of massive stellar flares on exoplanetary atmospheres and in assessing the variability of stars in TESS Sector Chromatic Indices. This research was conducted using data from the Kepler, TESS, GALEX, HST, IUE, and VOSPI observations of the Kepler-40 star, along with solar flare data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph and the Solar Dynamics Observatory. This finding has been made available in the form of an open-chapter publication titled Near-Ultraviolet Continuum of Stellar Flares, which includes this paper, along with six other related studies. This research was supported by NASA grants

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. These findings with the Jost function method have been compared to the traditional width analysis of the RPA Hamiltonian matrix, and the additional information obtained from the complex energy plane can be utilized to better comprehend the complex dynamics of this famous nuclear phenomenon. Double RPA calculations have allowed for the detailed characterization of each pole, revealing dense fluctuations from the $\Delta$ particle and the $1p$-$1h$ pair condensation that contribute to the residual width of the $^{16}$O giant resonance. These results highlight the Jost function method's capabilities in uncovering the intricate details of complex resonances and the dense fluctuations that give rise to their widths. The widespread applicability of this approach to complex eigenenergies within the RPA framework offers a valuable tool for nuclear physics research. The $^{16}$O data set has been made publicly available. The Jost function method relies on numerical roots of complex polynomials, and its development was influenced by the RPA linear system of equations and the physical constraints of the eigenenergies. The widespread applicability of this approach to complex eigenenergies within the RPA framework offers a valuable tool for nuclear physics research. The $^{16}$O data set has been made publicly available. The Wigner distribution functions of the dense fluctuations that contribute to the residual width of the $^{16}$O giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, are presented. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work's contribution sits at the intersection of clustering, influence estimation, and data-driven identification, and either alone or combined with other methods can provide valuable insights for experts in various fields. The research is supported by an open source Python toolbox available at: https://www.micc.ufrj.br/clusterinfluence.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that each dimension of the sparse code corresponds to a specific linguistic element, and by analyzing these codes, we can identify interesting patterns of language. All source code and datasets used in this study are publicly available at: https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN. For more information about text generation using GANs, the upcoming workshop paper "Text Generation using GANs: A Workshop Overview" provides a comprehensive overview of related work, along with guidelines and tips for conducting further research in this domain.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. The detection of interstellar panspermia would have far-reaching implications for a range of topics, from the distribution of life, planetary stability, and the role of stochastic events, to the potential for contaminated exoplanetary surfaces, astrobiology, and the ethics of searching for extra-terrestrial life. The approach taken here is applied to real data, with the outcome of analyzing a group of open star clusters revealing that one well-studied example may harbor evidence for interstellar panspermia. The proposed method provides a foundation for a broader project aimed at comprehensively explore the distribution of life within a specific star cluster, a mathematical model for which has been developed, but requires additional data to function effectively. The discovery that the phenomenon of interstellar panspermia could be observable in open star clusters, which are found to be capable of harboring life-bearing planets even in densely populated environments, also has significant implications for the question of whether life on Earth originated in this way. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture-specific models, offers guidelines for conducting such analyses, and provides a statistical tool for biologists to investigate ecological relationships between animals and their environment.  This tool is implemented in the R package SCRregSF.  We applied and tested this package using data from black-tailed prairie dogs, which demonstrated its effectiveness and statistical validity.  This package can be utilized for similar research on this species as well.  Furthermore, we discovered that capture-recapture models alone can recover parameters for resource selection functions, which has significant implications for conducting purely capture-based research on space usage. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. From a practical perspective, it offers a useful framework for researchers and engineers working with multilayer networks, especially in the context of electrical or mechanical systems comprising layered systems. Our study is further illustrated by examining a range of multilayer network scenarios, including small-scale networks and random networks with controlled characteristics. Our findings cover situations with single-layer networks, interlayer bridge connections, centralized connections, and a combination of small and large network components. Our research can be applied to these networks, all of which exhibit chaotic behavior. Our work also paves the way for a range of possible extensions, including the examination of the multilayer system's community structure, the introduction of random errors, and the exploration of different rotation angles. Moreover, our method has implications for the theory of Kuramoto oscillators, particularly in regards to the generation of the Jacobian matrix and the reduction of the multilayer system. Our code is publicly available online. Our research provides a novel approach for examining multilayer networks that can be extended to a broad range of systems and offers a promising foundation for future investigations. Our study sheds light on the complex dynamics underlying multilayer networks and reveals the mechanisms that give rise to both peaceful coexistence and violent symbiosis in these systems. Our findings indicate that the latter scenario is marked by the presence of large amplitude oscillations and chaotic behavior in at least one layer. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This research is also made relevant by comparing it to a modern context, such as conformal gravity. A notable finding is that the Einstein operator cannot be recovered from its image under the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, demonstrating that the differential module defined by the Einstein operator is not torsion-free and therefore the parameterization is not minimal. Consequently, the Einstein operator cannot be determined from this image, implying that the original statement attributed to Einstein is incorrect. On the other hand, the Cauchy stress operator can be recovered from its image under the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, making the parameterization of the Cauchy stress operator minimal, which also yields a novel approach to solving the direct problem for this operator. Additionally, this discovery leads to an overcomplication of the Einstein operator being simplified to the Bianchi operator, which in turn is equivalent to the Lelievre operator, a form that has not been previously reported. This research expands on an earlier, more concise version presented at a conference. The key results from that earlier work are the development of two key theorems, from which several important consequences follow. The first theorem is that the Einstein operator cannot be recovered from its image under the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, making the original statement attributed to Einstein incorrect. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles and concepts of this testing theory are presented here, demonstrating how its features can be used to fix errors and improving the quality of software. The approach has been tested with real-world programs written in C, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method. The development of this testing environment was facilitated by a research grant from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. The environment, called "DepCast", is available for download from the McGill University website. The research reported here was conducted within the context of the Canadian program of activity in trust-worthy computing. The development of reliable and safe software is paramount in today's technology-driven world. Although the use of sophisticated verification tools can help achieve this goal, their implementation is often hindered by the difficulty of setting up and understanding their underlying principles. In response to this challenge, a simple and intuitive testing environment called "DepTest" was developed to help programmers identify and fix mistakes found during testing. The environment provides a graphical representation of the errors and the corresponding code that can be navigated to pinpoint the areas that need adjustment. The effectiveness of this approach was tested with real-world programs written in C, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method. The approach has a straightforward and accessible design, allowing average programmers to use it, and is available for download from the McGill University website. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm is proven through a probabilistic argument, and we also compare it to a rival estimation algorithm previously developed to demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm in terms of accuracy. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand this method, offering users the opportunity to explore new aspects of numerical relativity. Solved examples in the code include solutions for scalar field perturbations and scalar clouds around rotating black holes, which can be visualized through 3D plots of the spacetime metric and conformal factor. As a landmark improvement, our research also introduces an innovative multigrid solver for a specific Hamiltonian constraint equation, involving a non-linear projection, which has implications for solving similar types of equations in mathematical physics. The developed code is available online, providing access to the underlying algorithms and an extensive set of numerical results. The Advancing Front technique has been successfully applied to divide the boundary of spatial slice boundaries, and an extensive examination of the code's performance has been conducted, showcasing the results of varying parametric options. The developed method has the potential to be adapted for use in time-domain simulations, and the underlying algorithms are anticipated to contribute to ongoing research in the numerical analysis of Hamiltonian constraints in mathematical physics. The code is capable of generating 3D plots from the extracted metric and conformal factor components, offering a graphical understanding of complex spacetime configurations. The code has been designed to serve as a starting point for further development, allowing user modification of key algorithms and providing access to the underlying code and numerical results. The developed code and the associated results provide a foundation for exploring fundamental field configurations in numerical relativity, including previously unexamined scenarios involving rotating black holes and fundamental field interactions. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a 5-fold change when subjecting the material to a magnetic field of varying intensity, and demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect can be accurately described using a phenomenological model. Moreover, we demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity can be assessed in experiments involving the measurement of the anomalous Hall effect, presenting a cost-effective method for investigating the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials. And finally, we demonstrate the potential of Mn$_3$NiN films for thermal to electrical energy conversion through the anomalous Nernst effect, and identify optimization pathways for this material in this application. And lastly, we conclude by outlining the experimental and theoretical approaches that can be utilized to investigate the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials, including the measure of thermal gradient distribution and finite element modeling, and the investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect through the measurement of the anomalous Hall effect. And further, we suggest potential research directions for exploring the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials, including the investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect at interfaces and the development of complex magnetic field patterns. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. We demonstrate this approach across scattering and spectroscopic measurements, including a resonant scattering experiment, and analyze a dataset from a scanning imaging experiment. The framework and models presented are accessible through the Bluesky Repository, an open-platform for sharing and managing research components. To facilitate further development and customization, the repository provides accessible code, along with documentation on the beamline setup and data reduction techniques used. The approach and framework introduced here serve as a foundation for developing and deploying machine learning applications at user facilities, enabling researchers to focus on developing models rather than setting up infrastructure. The extensive data collected at user facilities also provides a rich source of data for fair machine learning validation, with real-world applications at facilities like NSLS-II. The framework is available online at https://repository.bluesky.org/. The data analyzed in this study are available online at https://repository.bluesky.org/. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of projects that utilize composite materials, from aerospace to sports equipment.

The development of this technique and the proposed algorithm can also be applied to other applications of inverse problems and optimization, in addition to damage detection.

By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications. Furthermore, we conclude with the potential implications and limitations of this approach for more complex systems. Simpler elements often result in simpler systems, which in turn become more complex and insightful when individual knowledge is applied in specific ways, offering a rich and dynamic landscape that may offer valuable insights for various fields beyond physics. The underlying theory can be validated by observing the behavior of systems in real-life scenarios. The Lotka-Volterra model presented here has been thoroughly analyzed with numerical data verifying the predicted outcomes and providing additional information on system stability and key species population dynamics.
