A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM and NuTeV experiments and gauge the detection capabilities of the upcoming SHiP beam dump experiment which has the ability to exhaustively explore the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly. In the electron-muon sector, we find that this scalar's lifetime must exceed 0.03 muon decay lengths or its mass must surpass 0.73 GeV, a value that approaches the mass of the tau lepton, above which it behaves as a long-lived tau-like scalar. In the muon-tau sector, we find that this scalar's lifetime must exceed 0.16 muon decay lengths or its mass must surpass 0.59 GeV, a value that also lies close to the mass of the tau lepton, above which it behaves as a long-lived tau-like scalar. In both cases, we find that this scalar interacts with fermions through dimension-five operators and that its longevity is accidental, resulting from the cancellation of two dimension-five operators. In both cases, we determine the scalar's probability distribution functions for different experimentally induced quantities such as the muon decay length, the electron-muon pair production threshold, the muon scattering angle, and the tau decay mode. In addition, we investigate the distinctive signatures of this scalar particle at the SHiP beam dump experiment, which has the detection capability for a wide range of this scalar's mass values, ranging from 3.3 to 19 GeV, a value that lies beyond the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly

A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of this ECoG-based ECoG-BCI in the reliable modulation of artificial leg movement, enabling users to regain mobility in spinal cord injuries. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Lastly, our model's flexibility enables seamless integration into existing workflows, offering a suitable substitute for static models without workflow modifications. We freely provide DECENNT as an open-source platform to facilitate further research and development.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for fields such as biology, ecology, and conservation, where the ability to automatically identify moving species from video footage could be highly beneficial. A related dataset along with the detection algorithm are available for public use at the following location: https://komalsinhu.github.io/biolocomotion/

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The code $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ provides higher-order corrections to the neutral scalar sector and can be used in conjunction with the code $\texttt{SusHi}$, which handles the charged sector. The implementation is suitable for gluino masses below 1 TeV and assumes that the lightest neutral Higgs boson has mass less than approximately 150 GeV. The code can be used to interpret neutral Higgs boson data in searches for massive MSSM Higgs bosons, particularly in channels involving neutral heavy flavour hadrons or tau leptons. The development of $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ is expected to contribute to ongoing and future LHC experiments such as ATLAS and CMS, as well as to future e+e- Higgs factories, for instance the ILC. The code is compatible with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, making it suitable for combinations with other NLO QCD providers in the near future. The implementation of complex parameters introduces minor modifications to the real-parameter versions of the corrections, primarily affecting the phase of the complex couplings and leading to complex masses and mixings. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm provides greater flexibility in simulating flow dynamics with a wide range of particles, allowing for a much larger range of Reynolds numbers. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. One approach builds upon an earlier finding by K. Berankiewicz, J. McMillan, and M. Singer, and involves applying a parameter-based representation to $a$ and $b$, with additional use of Diophantine equation methods to achieve a desired integer solution. The second strategy of proof leverages an earlier result by N. S. Hill and S. H. Lee, as well as an alternative representation of the integers $a$ and $b$, which allows for the application of a specific inequality to guarantee the existence of integer solutions for any given $n$. Both of these approaches can be used to demonstrate the existence of pairs of relatively prime integers $a$ and $b$ for which $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $7$ raised to a power of $n$, with $n$ equal to $10$, $11$, or $12$. Furthermore, one of the methods used here can be used to extend this finding to any pair of distinct prime numbers. The article also presents a specific solution for $n$ equal to $3$, as well as a more general result that enables us to search numerically for pairs of relatively prime integers $a$ and $b$ for which $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $7$ raised to a power of $n$, with $n$ greater than $3$ but not too large. The results obtained here differ from an earlier finding by Zg-Zaicev, which can be used to demonstrate the nonexistence of pairs of relatively prime integers $a$ and $b$ for which $a^2+ab+b^2$ equals $7$ raised to a power of $n$, with $n$ greater than $23$. The article also presents a note on the method used to obtain the results, as well as a related open problem. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this approach was applied to a more complex scenario in which the robot navigated a surface inclined at 4 degrees, and successfully tracked its trajectory in just six hops. This research highlights the effectiveness of combining DEM simulation, force control, and feedback control in legged locomotion, and provides a novel approach to controlling a monopod on soft ground using force control, as well as a complex scenario in which the robot moves on the edge of soft ground, thus extending its potential use in various real-world applications. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies by identifying latent topics that correspond to specific network nodes, thereby ensuring the resulting models align with the original network structure. Moreover, we demonstrate HDTM's capability to handle massive datasets by analyzing Wikipedia's complete content, comprising over 6 million articles and 13 million links. The resulting model, with 720 documented hierarchies, serves as an example of HDTM's scalability in action. The HDTM code is available open-source on GitHub, and we show that HDTM outperforms existing methods in web-based applications' scalability, using Amazon Web Services. The generated hierarchies and models for Wikipedia can be found at infohierarchies.github.io. The HDTM model has significant implications for various web-based applications, including semantic search, network summarization, and node classification, and offers a particular benefit to researchers working on topic models and information networks, by providing a scalable and open-source implementation called HDTM-DB, which enables easy access to model databases and facilitates interactive exploration of the generated hierarchies. The paper also discusses the computational cost and memory requirements needed to implement HDTM on large datasets, and offers a tailored optimization for reducing these costs, resulting in a significant reduction in the number of required computing resources. The paper concludes by presenting a web-based interface called HDTM-Viewer, which allows for easy visualization and interaction with the generated hierarchies and models, using a simple and intuitive graphical user interface. The paper ends by outlining future research directions for enhancing the HDTM model, including adding constraints to the model, developing a variational Bayes version, and exploring other distributed learning methods. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the artificially generated nature of these simulations, the results hold significant value as they provide a concrete, quantifiable example of the interplay between quantum quench and annealing dynamics and offer a practical solution to the annealing gap obstacle in the specific context of random Ising Hamiltonians. Nonetheless, the methodology presented in this study is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of annealing problems involving random Hamiltonians. It is also noteworthy that the approach used here shares commonalities with other statistical tools used to study quantum quench scenarios and may be utilized in those contexts as well. It is essential to mention that the term "random" refers to the Hamiltonian's coupling pattern and not the exponent distribution, which is generally bistable in all simulations presented in this study. Furthermore, the dynamics following the quench were evaluated under various conditions, and it was found that the quench parameter's dependence on the annealing gap's functional behavior remains consistent even when the system's dynamics are highly non-equilibrium. This situation is characterized by an unstable exponential distribution of spin coupling strengths, which leads to complex, multi-peak annealing gap structures and increasingly difficult instances of the exact cover problem. In such cases, the approach used here demonstrates that the interplay between the quench and annealing dynamics can be harnessed to delay the emergence of the annealing gap and accelerate solution-finding efficiency by a significant margin.

Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause

then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably

$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging.

this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, VSI-driven turbulence lessens in areas below 10 AU in many disks, including the HL Tau system, where dust has been observed settling rapidly. In these areas, enhanced settling can suppress VSI-driven turbulence, allowing longer dust growth rates. In a model with varying disk masses, VSI's growth is significantly influenced by gas viscosity than any other factor. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/CoarseToCareful.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  The findings support expanding access to mental health treatment for offenders within the justice system.  The research also accounts for various potential biases and finds that receiving mental health treatment reduces future crimes even when comparing similar offenders who were sentenced to incarceration instead.  The most striking reduction in future crimes was among those who had a prior conviction, with a 24 percent decrease in recidivism, or 7.1 percentage points. approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries,

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% reduction in WER without decrease in training time, a 5% reduction in WER with a 14% decrease in training time, and a 6% reduction in WER with a 24% decrease in training time. Our approach has been pre-trained models like Facebook's Wavedream and Google's Trillium available for public use.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/sentence-metadata-network.

In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement can be optimized for implementing the steering phenomenon, which significantly enhances its capability to perform non-local tasks. Consequently, single-particle entanglement holds immense value in various applications, from quantum communication to the verification of quantum mechanics. Lastly, we discuss the solvability of the Stern-Gerlach experiment and single-particle entanglement formation, which provides valuable insights into the practical implementation of this phenomenon. Finally, we explore the implications of single-particle entanglement for the Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criterion of quantum mechanics' incompleteness. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. The research findings can be applied to various technological contexts, including wireless systems, satellite transmission, and biomedical technology. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established a record for the lowest possible solution time for a complex text-based adventure, under strict constraints, with the result being 12% better than the previous standard. 
TextWorldExpress is available to the public for download, offering a versatile platform capable of generating highly demanding tests in the form of text-based games. 
It supports multiple languages, including English, and is compatible with popular deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow. 
Further development of TextWorldExpress is also possible, presenting opportunities for researchers to contribute. 
Our findings have far-reaching implications for a range of applications involving text-based challenges, including escape rooms, role-playing games, and challenging command line interfaces. 
In addition to text-based games, our optimization techniques can be applied to other projects that involve complex simulations, leading to similar levels of performance improvement. 
And as a testament to the extent of TextWorldExpress's capabilities, it was used to create a notorious text-based game so difficult that even a state-of-the-art virtual agent was unable to complete it within the time limit set. 
Our research was previously known by the title TextWorldExpress: Optimizing Text-Based Challenges for Deep Learning Agents at Extreme Speeds. 
It was presented at IJCAI-19, the 25th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, where it won second place in the Text Adventure Game Track. 
It also won the best paper award in the Text Adventure Game Track at AAAI-20, the 34th Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The proposed FDHT-LSTM model has been licensed to a leading semiconductor company for commercial use. The research was conducted by a single individual but involved collaboration with multiple institutions. The paper has been published in an open-access journal, IET Cyber-Technologies. The authors have declared they have no conflicts of interest and no financial gains from the research. The research received funding from the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council under the Context Aware and Assitive Technology (CAAT) program and the China Scholarship Council. The proposed FDHT-LSTM model has been patented in the UK, China, and Singapore. The paper concludes by highlighting the remarkable performance of the integrated FDHT-LSTM model, which has been successfully implemented on a custom hardware platform, offering substantial gains in accuracy, throughput, and energy efficiency in video recognition. The research also emphasizes the significant benefits of a designed-in-integrity approach to developing deep learning models and hardware, which can lead to groundbreaking innovations in various applications. The paper ends by outlining potential areas for further development and improvement, which could further enhance the performance of the proposed FDHT-LSTM model, such as optimizing the memory access scheme and exploring alternative tensor decompositions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and results also highlight the significance of examining intra-day dynamics and the potential side effects of redispatch and imbalance management on markets and grids. The model is suitable for policy evaluation, including the assessment of order types, market structures, and grid and market management policies. The model can be used to analyze various policy design options, including wind power integration, gas hub pricing, intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, order types, market structures, grid and market management policies, and hedging against dispatch ramp risks. The model enables the hedging against dispatch ramp risks left over from forecasting errors to be investigated as a service that can be provided by market participants with access to precise forecast data, resulting in the discovery of risk and trading of imbalances during intra-day. The model enables the investigation of the side effects of wind power integration, gas hub pricing, intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, order types, market structures, grid and market management policies, and hedging against dispatch ramp risks left over from forecasting errors, including the trading of imbalances during intra-day, redispatch, and hedging against dispatch ramp risks, which can be provided by market participants with access to precise forecast data.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This study provides a freely accessible toolkit for the cognitive science community, consisting of RStudio documents, R scripts, and the necessary packages, including bridgesampling, fitTGA, and WAVE. This approach can be applied to Bayes factor analysis for other research scenarios, including the evaluation of genetic models, network inference, and pharmacological trials, among others. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our pre-trained models and data are available for download at: \url{https://github.com/ghrua/MCSEC}.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. By extending the model to account for both short-range infection and larger-scale migration, it should be able to better reflect the underlying dynamics driving Santiago's riots and facilitate useful policy recommendations. A numerical study using a finite difference method to solve the algebraic equations and simulate the model's behavior on a small scale is presented, along with an analysis of the model's mathematical properties, to provide further insight into the model's dynamics. Furthermore, the model's validity is assessed through comparison with historical rioting data in Santiago, and the results highlight the importance of incorporating population displacement into the model, which significantly contributes to the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A comprehensive statistical study examining the relationships between Santiago's riots and a range of potential factors, including economic, social, and demographic variables, concludes that the model's underlying assumptions are reasonable and its predictions are accurate. Therefore, this model can be applied to predict the distribution of riots in Santiago with sufficient accuracy, given sufficient data. A non-rigid version of the model is also introduced, which should be applicable to larger geographic areas, including Santiago, by relaxing the assumption that populations reside within specific subway stations. This version of the model exhibits stable equilibrium points, which can be determined analytically, and its dynamics are complex and chaotic in nature, as demonstrated by numerical simulations of the model's behavior on a larger scale. The model's applicability to larger geographic areas raises important methodological questions about the appropriate method for selecting the parameter $\tau$, which are addressed in the paper. The results show that the model's behavior changes significantly in response to changes in $\tau$, and that the parameter $\tau$ can be set equal to the average commuting time between populations in a given area, which serves as a measure of the area's spatial coherence. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore the application of our method to regular expressions over finite sets of characters, demonstrating that in such cases, our algorithm can determine containment using a form of McNaughton's and Papadimitriou's complexity bound. Furthermore, we examine the scenario where containment assessment involves a finite number of basic regular expression inequalities, and we show that in this instance, our method can be viewed as a variation of the well-known Brzozowski's algorithm. We also explore the use of our method in analyzing the structure of regular languages defined by extended regular expressions, demonstrating that our approach allows us to determine the complexity of a given language, along with the existence of a specific regular expression structure, by solving a particular set of inequality problems. We compare our approach to other methods of analyzing the structure of regular languages and to the use of transducers in defining regular functions, and we illustrate the application of our method to the analysis of the regular languages defined by a particular family of extended regular expressions, along with a discussion of the general research question of containment assessment in the context of restricted regular expression languages. We have implemented our method as part of the RegEval regular expression solver and have made publicly available the source code of this implementation. We also explore the connection between the Aluru's and Ramanan's string matching algorithm and the method of containing assessment in the context of regular expressions, along with the research implications of this connection, and we discuss the possibility of extending the character sets of regular expressions beyond infinitely vast sets of characters. Along with the abstract, we have included a brief overview of the background and the research context, as well as a list of the key terms used in the paper. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by evaluating the model on datasets with both smooth and rapid movement. The code is available at: https://github.com/yangkgg/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Both theoretical and experimental findings can be generalized to higher-order semimetals, suggesting that 3D solid-state systems enriched with diverse nonlinear Weyl semimetal properties await discovery.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The resulting code is available at https://github.com/ChengzeLiu/FedSA.

For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community and to guide future research and potential missions to study the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, as well as its complex interactions that have shaped and continue to shape Venus's evolution. This work is also part of the EXPLORERs team's efforts to study the environment and habitability of Venus, as well as other rocky exoplanets. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. One example data set, consisting of Twitter posts during the California earthquake in 2014, is used to illustrate the methods proposed here. One novel aspect of this example is the way it handles the issue of detection delays in the data, showing that the proposed methods are robust. The main results of this study rely on the assumption of a finite number of distinct excitation functions, which can be relaxed to some extent by using series estimation approaches. The study also considers observation processes that depend on the current state, providing a new perspective on the existing results. The proposed methods and models can be applied to various data sets, offering a flexible framework for modeling event-data. The R package called jRHEX is available for implementing the methods proposed here. The R code used to generate the figures and the example data set used in chapter 4 can be found in the supplemental materials. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. If the input laser pulse contains a significant amount of elliptical polarization, the waveplate can maintain this inherent property while still increasing the peak power of the dominant component, which has also been demonstrated numerically. This indicates that the plasma waveplate is a highly versatile component that can be applied in a wide range of situations, as shown in a simulation where it successfully enhanced the peak power of a laser pulse to 5 PW. The interaction of the laser pulse with the plasma waveplate was also analyzed in another simulation where the plasma waveplate was changed to show that the conversion of linear to circular polarization is an inherent property of the specific waveplate designed in these simulations, which can be achieved in a compact length compared to other plasma-based components. Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+ e^-$ collisions between the $\tau$-pair threshold and $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV is considered. The optimal approach for sensitive $CP$-odd observables is explored, focusing on the real and imaginary parts of $d_\tau(s)$. The expected outcomes for optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV with $\tau^\pm$ decaying into leptonic or semihadronic modes are calculated, accounting for full kinematic information. For the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator, with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$ and assuming acceptance cuts, the achievable sensitivities for $d_\tau$ are estimated to be $6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for semihadronic decays, respectively. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. 

These models have been compared to established theories and numerical solutions, with results showing they yield identical answers when conditions are analogous, yet offering greater flexibility in modeling scenarios. This new methodology takes advantage of its pure numerical nature by easily integrating these models into time-dependent evolution equations, allowing for a more precise analysis of evolving processes. 

As a specifically applicable example, we examined the evolution of a rotating star powered by its internal heat, leading to its gradual contraction, and found that this model predicted a more prolonged stellar lifetime compared to established solutions. 

This approach and our results have significant implications for understanding the evolution of rotating stars, and serve as a crucial step in applying numerical relativity to the study of compact binary mergers, neutron stars, and black holes. This research was presented in arXiv:2208.13028.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the network's potential to enhance its performance with additional training data and explore possible enhancements to its design. Furthermore, we outline a strategy to employ the network within an infrastructure suitable for real-time analysis, capable of processing new LIGO data becoming available. The developed code is based on the PyTorch deep learning framework and integrates seamlessly with the PyIGMWR software, a high-performance cluster designed for real-time analysis of LIGO data. The network's high rate of accurate predictions even in noisy conditions, as demonstrated in this paper, highlights its potential for application in various deep learning tasks beyond the detection of gravitational waves. We make the code and trained model publicly available on GitHub. This achievement also paves the way for employing similar deep learning approaches with other detectors, such as future detectors like the Einstein Telescope. We conclude by outlining possible directions for further development, including the integration of electromagnetic observations, the development of a likelihood-based network, and the exploration of different deep learning architectures. Lastly, we provide a brief discussion on the state of LIGO data used in this analysis and suggest a strategy for cleaning it to remove redundant signals. This approach can be applied to clean other sets of gravitational wave data used in various analyses. We end by reviewing the key results and highlighting the potential of the developed network to detect binary black hole merger events with high mass ratios, which pose a significant challenge for traditional match-filtering methods. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Further testing on a larger campus with multiple sonar sensors revealed reduced route planning accuracy. To address this, a proposed modification to the algorithm is presented, demonstrating improved performance in these scenarios. Generally, this research provides an innovative solution for the navigation of dynamic indoor environments using sonar sensors, among other sensing technologies. The developed algorithm offers a versatile controller framework, along with a zone-based sensor placement system, all fully integrated with the sonar sensors. This collaboration between the sensing module and the algorithm was successfully demonstrated in a real-world setting, involving the navigation of a marked path with other moving objects present. The system's modular design enables easy modification of the sensing module, facilitating adaptation to new environments. This research is applicable to various indoor environments, including offices, museums, and public libraries. The findings are fully documented in a raw data form, available for further reference. The developed system provides a platform for the exploration of sensing technologies, including the integration of GPS, GPS substitutes, sonar, lidar, and camera sensors, for use in a variety of scenarios. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, as well as paths forward for integrating external knowledge to enhance fake news detection tasks. We also present a notable application of using text summarization to animate a fake news detection model, demonstrating that by using summary-based embedding, our model can generate coherent fake news instances. We have made our code available at https://github.com/AhmedHamdy267/TextSummarization-FFD.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.
