High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework under an permissive license to facilitate easy adoption and experimentation by a range of developers.  In addition to DynaSOAr, we established a set of guidelines called SOAR principles that are applicable to all object-oriented GPU programming, including applications beyond the SMMO category.  These general principles, which are compatible with existing guidelines, offer a simpler and more efficient way to convert object-oriented algorithms to the SOAR format, and provide a roadmap for further speedup and efficiency gains with smaller benchmark applications.  Our results show that DynaSOAr and the SOAR principles can achieve performance improvements and reduce memory usage and fragmentation in a range of object-oriented GPU applications, including popular and widely used benchmarks.  We believe that DynaSOAr and the SOAR principles have the potential to revive interest in the efficient GPU programming of object-oriented applications, and we are available to provide further support and guidance to interested developers.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework, the SOAR principles, and related documentation under easy-to-access links.  As a result of our research, we identified a range of research opportunities and challenges presented in the paper's conclusion section.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell sizing in order to obtain reliable results, as an under-sized supercell led to errors including anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. Furthermore, the design includes a straightforward over-voltage protection mechanism, enabling it to handle dynamic voltage scaling, and a wide temperature range of -100{\deg}C to 100{\deg}C with some limitations. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Such investigation will be crucial in clarifying the degree to which the core mass function influences the resulting star formation's mass.  Such an understanding is critical to better defining the factors that determine the massive star formation rate within molecular clouds.  On top of that, it also raises the question of whether massive star formation can originate from cores with mass similar to that of the cloud's overall mean, rather than being limited to the most massive cores.  Finally, it is essential to monitor the mass evolution of these cores over time in order to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how core mass growth contributes to massive star formation, and to also probe the timescales involved in this process.  This study's findings are based on the assumption that the associated outflows are accurate markers of the cores that will eventually form massive stars.  While such assumption is not universally accepted, it is widely acknowledged that outflows are associated with cores that have some chance of forming massive stars, even if the exact probability is unknown.  Therefore, the analysis may be viewing a selective sample of cores that have the strongest potential for forming massive stars, and as such the observed mass growth may be more pronounced in this group.  Further research is necessary to fully enumerate all cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud, as well as to carry out a similar analysis of their associated outflows, and to then compare the mass distributions of protostellar and starless cores for each outflow's associated cores, for a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics.  On top of that, it is essential to investigate the relationship between the mass growth and the associated outflows, as well as the surrounding environment and its influence on the mass growth, in order to better define the factors that determine the massive star formation rate within molecular clouds

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achievement ensures IShTAR can accurately replicate conditions necessary for understanding and preventing plasma degradation in helical devices powered by ICRF waves.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology simplifies the evaluation of detected nuclei, as it allows for accurate evaluation based on binary masks, rather than dense masks that are more difficult to annotate correctly. The proposed W-Net architecture has been thoroughly tested and its effectiveness proven through a comparison with state-of-the-art models, including U-Net, ANU-Net, LEAN-Net, and a two-stage U-Net model. The results show that the proposed W-Net model outperforms these models in terms of evaluation metrics such as the IOU score and precision. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A software implementation of GCNNs, specifically a simple GCNN, is also developed and made available for public use. A real-world application to a well-known face recognition dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of this intuitive analysis. A comparative assessment of the derived slim GCNN against a standard GCNN reveals that while the complex GCNN initially performs better, the simpler version closes the gap with increased data. A high overall accuracy rate of 96.5% is achieved on a challenging face recognition task using just 64 dimensions. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results show a 13.44 dB boost in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and a 10.95 dB boost in mean structured similarity (SSIM) in simulation data and a 12.75 dB SNR boost and a 10.27 dB SSIM boost in experimental data following the application of VSSA. These outcomes underline the advantages of VSSA SA in elastography, facilitating accurate estimation of lateral tissue displacement. The technique's potential for enhancing elastography is further highlighted via an analytical discussion. The code for VSSA SA beamforming and OVERWIND elastography has been developed using MATLAB and C++ and is presented in the appendix. The outcomes of this study also suggest possible optimisation paths for the technique. The results of this research have been previously presented at conferences, namely the 2020 IEEE International Ultrasonics Symposium and the 2020 British Conference of Medical Ultrasonics. The outcomes of this research have further extensions in the form of improved VSSA, deep learning-based OVERWIND, and data augmentation, that have been presented in the additional files. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that imperative algorithms are, in fact, a type of natural deduction proofs, and to explore the relationship between forward and backward reasoning. In doing so, we introduce logical pseudocodes as a means of connecting algorithms with proofs, and show that forward reasoning can lead to explicit conditions for ensuring correctness and safety. Additionally, we show that natural deduction proofs are equivalent to natural deduction logical pseudocodes, and demonstrate the relationship between forward and backward reasoning by comparing natural and natural extension deduction logical pseudocodes. Furthermore, we provide an example of natural extension deduction logical pseudocodes in the form of a natural deduction framework, and show that it is possible to derive the conditions for correctness and safety from a given specification using natural extension deduction logical pseudocodes. Our results can be seen as a form of execution models based on the natural extension deduction logic, which allows for execution of proofs as well as verification of specifications. Our research also leads to an expanded definition of web pages, which we call "logical pseudocode pages," and provide an example of a simple logical pseudocode page. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We achieve this result using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method, and our analysis focuses on a simplified case to showcase the underlying principles of our approach. Furthermore, we provide a more sophisticated algorithm with storage capacity of $k \times \poly(d,\Delta)$ dimensions for the general scenario, and demonstrate the existence of an optimal coreset with a specific structure, which can be efficiently realized with our algorithm. As for the space-efficient variant, we outline a path for its construction within our general algorithm framework. We also discuss a batch version of our algorithm, as well as a method for updating coreset points when data points are modified, by utilizing a combination of our algorithm and the concept of heavy objects. We derive our results using a novel, probabilistic sampling method, and a an explicit construction of an optimal coreset, which serves as a foundation for understanding our general algorithm and provides a way to create a coreset for a related, slightly larger dataset. We also compare our results with those of existing research, which are based on storage capacity of a polynomial in the target data dimension, showing that our algorithm for a single pass exceeds the storage limit of a polynomial in data dimensions and instead utilizes a polynomial in the base-2 logarithm of the target delta. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by focusing on macro-actions, our model can be adapted for application in large-scale real-world scenarios, including in robotics. All the code used in this research is publicly available. We expand the hierarchical model to dynamic grids, providing a valuable tool for, for example, optimizing paths for surveillance missions. From the experimental results, we also derive a straightforward formula to predict the expected termination time of hierarchical pursuit-evasion games. We conclude by outlining possible future hierarchical developments, including integration with deep learning technologies. This work is categorized in the field of hierarchical reinforcement learning, with a specific focus on stochastic games. We suggest several future research projects, including integrating hierarchical learning with existing off-the-shelf pursuit-evasion algorithms, developing a more precise formula to predict expected termination times, and exploring alternatives to the reward-based aggregation method. We propose a straightforward prediction formula for the expected game duration, which can be utilized by researchers in related fields. In addition, we provide an illustration of a possible future scenario involving dynamic hierarchical grids, which we refer to as 'trek-based grids'. These new grids offer an innovative way of representing complex, variable environments and can be simply visualized as specialized graphs. We suggest several possible names for the term 'trek', which is central to this new concept, including 'path', 'route', 'trail', 'course', and 'journey'. We propose a method for predicting the expected time required to complete a specified task within these trek-based environments, which can be calculated by multiplying the length of the trek by the average time needed to handle individual nodes. We demonstrate this prediction method through a simulated game, which matches the predicted outcome with the result obtained from actual gameplay. We also examine the relationship between the length of the trek and the expected time required to complete the task, which can be approximated by a linear function according to our results. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that separating tasks with modular networks
can prevent performance degradation and achieve high success rates in complex
multi-task environments. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach facilitates
smooth transfer learning when moving from a single-task to a multi-task setting. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/MMDMS.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By combining these results, we derive several notable consequences and generalizations, including an undecidability result for certain formal systems and an unprovability statement for a specific arithmetic formula. This study's aim is to reveal the internal connections among these seminal theorems and demonstrate the cohesive nature of first-order arithmetic proofs. Moreover, we examine the initial reaction of logicians to these results and the development of the field since then. In concluding, this study is motivated by the insights gained from analyzing the relationship among Godel's and Tarski's pioneering work, and the profound impact it had on shaping the field of mathematical logic. This study's results have been presented at the conference "Incompleteness in the 21st Century" held in Munich, Germany from July 25-28, 2016, where researchers including Willem A. Harvey, George Boolos, and Yuri I. Manin offered their insights among other contributions. This paper is a combination of my own work and that of my conference colleagues. As such, I have made considerable revisions to the original manuscript to incorporate the suggestions provided by my conference colleagues. This revised version now presents a more comprehensive exploration of the subject matter. This paper is aimed at mathematical logic experts and the general philosophical community, and is directed at readers with an interest in the historical development and current applications of the underlying theories. This paper consists of three main parts, each of which can be read independently. The first part combines the proofs of Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem, Tarski's Undefinability Theorem, the Diagonal Lemma, and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem, and presents a overview of the underlying principles and the techniques used in the proofs. The second part explores the consequences of these results, and the third part examines the change in logicians' reaction to these results and the development of the field since then. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of sampled images and reduced the gap between the distribution of sampled images and the baseline estimated posterior distribution. This was visible in visual assessments and more rigorously confirmed through higher dimensionality Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics. We made publicly available the code and models used in this research. The GAN training details, combined with the theoretical analysis of the model's properties, can be found in the supplementary materials. The baseline estimated posterior distribution was estimated using a regularized Markov chain Monte Carlo, and we presented two applications: MRI imaging with multiple coils, and image inpainting with partially revealed images. The evaluation showed that the sampled images based on the proposed method, the current state of the art, and the baseline model are indistinguishable, according to expert visual assessments. However, the proposed method generated more diverse images, based on the inception metric, while the baseline model produced higher quality images, based on the Fr\'{e}chet metric, in both evaluation tests. The proposed method successfully sampled 64x64 MRI images from the posterior distribution, with a quality that was comparable to the baseline model, based on the evaluation tests. The proposed method, the current state of the art, and the baseline model produced MRI images of the same quality, based on the evaluation tests, but the proposed method generated more diverse images, based on the inception metric, in both evaluation tests. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The contribution of this current work extends that of a preceding study, from which it differs by incorporating novel approaches to invariant configuration specification. We conclude by reviewing the method of searching for invariant configurations and presenting two key results related to the nonexistence of invariant manifolds in fractional-order systems. The article is organized to facilitate the ease of understanding of these results for readers with minimal background in mathematics. We use straightforward and concise language throughout the paper. The main topic of this work, the nonexistence of invariant manifolds in fractional-order systems, was first demonstrated in a preceding study, from which we differ by having a system whose dynamics are described by the fractional order differential equation of the form (1.1) ddtx(t) = (1 - μ)αx(t) + μβx(τt) + f(x(t), x(τt)), where 0 < α, β ≤ 1, and examine this system in the neighborhood of an equilibrium point. The approach we used in the preceding study of defining the invariant manifold as the set containing all system states that maintain zero asymptotic behavior, we obtained the condition F(0) = 0 for the invariant manifold, which we further simplified to f(0, 0) = 0. We then determined the stability of the equilibrium point under the action of the system with the invariant manifold, which we found to be associated with the stability of the system given by the equation ddtx(t) = f(x(t), x(t)). We demonstrated that the system with the invariant manifold is asymptotically stable if it is globally asymptotically stable, which we further showed implies that the system with the invariant manifold must be fractional for any α, β ∈ (0, 1). The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, calculations determine the distance to this screen as well as the extent and characteristics of the void, contributing to the mapping of the Local Bubble's structure. The proximity of this screen to the solar system also becomes evident through the analysis of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit, with predictions made for similar observations of other pulsars with similar properties. The methods employed in this research can be applied broadly to pulsar pulse profiles and various screens within the interstellar medium. The extensive data set examined in this paper remains raw data available for further study. The findings presented in this paper contribute to the understanding of the Local Bubble and the mapping of the interstellar medium, with the associated data accessible via the National Radio Astronomy Observatory's Data Archive Server. The observed timescales of vacuum scintillation effects on pulse profiles at high frequencies indicate small charge densities in the screen, which can be quantified as approximately 10^(-13) g/cm^3, or the equivalent of a few solar masses scattered over the 5.46 parsecs distance to the screen. The extensive data set examined in this paper can be utilized for various purposes, with examples provided in the appendix. The methodology employed in this research can be applied to other pulsar pulse profiles and associated screens within the interstellar medium. The proximity of the solar system to this screen becomes evident through the analysis of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit, with predictions made for similar observations of other pulsars with similar properties. The findings presented in this paper contribute to the understanding of the Local Bubble and the mapping of the interstellar medium, with the associated data accessible via the National Radio Astronomy Observatory's Data Archive

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Human evaluator ratings reveal that the proposed method exceeds the baseline WN model in terms of quality and pitch accuracy for unseen frequency inputs. Moreover, QPNet matches the baseline in terms of quality but surpasses it in terms of pitch accuracy for inputs within the frequency range. Code available at: https://github.com/Parandkuhi/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, the theory of shadows is shown to be responsive to funisectors, compatible with composition, and enabled for the computation of shadows for funisectors representing monoids. The theory of shadows is also found to be responsive to the structure of the circle, resulting in the recognition of its structure as a trace, and this circle structure can be utilized to define a trace on a bicategory. The concept of shadows is then compared to the theory of traces, with the theory of shadows equivalent to the theory of traces for bicategories, although this equivalence requires the utilization of a specific model. The compatibility of funisectors with shadows of a bicategory is expressed through the composition of funisectors in shadows, and this composition is proven to be equivalent to the composition of funisectors in traces, resulting in the recognition of the structure of the circle in traces as monoidal. The theory of shadows of a bicategory is also found to be responsive to the inclusion of the circle, enabling the derivation of traces from funisectors representing monoids. The theory of shadows is then applied to the computation of shadows for the group algebra of the symmetric group on n variables, resulting in the recognition of its structure as the endomorphism functor of the standard module for the quantum group U_q(s_n). The theory of shadows is then applied to the computation of shadows for the group algebra of the braid group B_n, resulting in the recognition of its structure as the intersection of the inner asymptote of the dual of the standard module for the quantum group U_q(s_n) with the action of the braid group B_n, although this result requires the utilization of a specific model. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zhoukui, along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset accessible at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/data/vggsound_source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/JinHePro/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and we treat it as a weak solution inverse problem, defining the stability estimate in the $L^2$ norm. This study also outlines numerical methods to solve the problem, including a gradient-type iterative algorithm and a conjugate gradient iterative method using a regularization approach. We demonstrate the feasibility of these methods with numerical experiments. This research was presented at the 3rd International Conference on Inverse Problems, held in Cairo, Egypt in 2018. A previous short communication on this work was shared at the 2nd International Conference on Inverse Problems, held in Moscow, Russia in 2016. A related project involving a control problem for the same model was presented at the 1st International Conference on Inverse Problems, held in Istanbul, Turkey in 2014. All three conferences were organized by the European Mathematical Society. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of South Africa, the South African National Research Foundation, the University of Pretoria, the Centre for Research in Mathematical and Computational Sciences, and the South African National Research Foundation. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we derive equations for the impulse control point
and the elasticity of delay discounting, and these expressions facilitate the
interpretation of the model's elements in terms of impulsivity. Our model's
statistics enable us to examine the implications of a perfect correlation between
impulsivity and delay discounting, and we find that a certain level of
diversity in impulsivity is necessary to explain certain behavioral patterns. This
necessary level of diversity can arise from the optimal policy's robustness
property, which is influenced by the shape of the impulsivity distribution. We
also explore the relationship between our model and existing exponential delay
discounting models, including the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting model, and
these comparisons reveal that the average and standard deviation of impulsivity
can take on specific values that result in these models. Last but not least, we
derive the probability density function of the optimal delay, and this density
fits the Tsallis distribution when the delay is expressed on a logarithmic scale. 
Our model's unique features provide novel insights into the relationship between
impulsivity and delay discounting, and these insights are unlike the results
obtained using the existing exponential delay discounting models. We also find
that the diversity in impulsivity is necessary for explaining the observed
asymmetry between the probability of choosing the immediate reward and the

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This specific gauge choice can be achieved through a direct transformation of the standard linearized Riemann tensor, which might be advantageous for higher derivative theories such as $f(R)$ gravities.  We also examine the implications for the linearized gravitational field equations derived from an action of a general $f(R)$ gravity, demonstrating that one particular harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with five degrees of freedom.  However, we note that this particular harmonic gauge leads to a deformed linearized Riemann tensor, and using the conventional definition may result in the wrong conclusion.  Finally, we demonstrate that both the linearized massive gravity model and the $f(R)$ gravity can be analyzed through the formalism of covariant perturbations of general relativity.  We also examine the implications for the specific $f(R)$ gravity model given by $f(R) = R  - (R^2)/p^2$, which reduces to the linearized massive gravity model when expanded to the next-to-leading order.  However, we note that this model is not stable in the deep infrared regime due to the presence of a negative mass squared term, which results in a scalar degree of freedom becoming asymptotically free.  This encourages further investigation of this model, which might be accessible through numerical or analytical means such as the use of regulated delta functions or flow equations.  We also examine the implications for the specific $f(R)$ gravity model given by $f(R) = R  - (R^2)/p^2$ in the high energy regime, which is comparable to the Einstein power-law gravity model with $\gamma = 1$. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to traditional, purely analytical explanations. A previous study by other authors, which examined the implications of negative absolute temperature for a two-level system within quantum mechanics, is also discussed. Although their focus was primarily on the concept's theoretical foundations, they found that the average occupation number approach can lead to misinterpretation, especially in situations where the energy distribution is uncertain. Therefore, they advocated for the use of the Boltzmann distribution in its unaltered form to avoid such misconceptions. Within this report, the relationship between the average occupation number and the Boltzmann distribution is examined, with an emphasis on showcasing the connection between these concepts through graphical means, specifically for the energy levels of a two-level system. This approach may offer undergraduate students a visual understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. A notable finding by other authors, which showed that the average occupation number approach can result in the average energy of the system being positive even when the majority of the system's energy is occupied by a small subset of particles that have extremely high energies, is also discussed. This result is illustrated through graphical means, with an emphasis on presenting the distribution of the energy occupation versus the average energy per particle. A comparison is made between the average occupation number and the energy distribution of a two-level system, with an emphasis on highlighting the potential for misinterpretation that can arise from the average occupation number alone. This report also examines the situation where the energy distribution is uncertain or ill-defined, with an emphasis on examining the potential consequences for the understanding of negative absolute temperature. A proposal is made to modify the average occupation number by using the specific heat capacity instead, which can provide a better, more accurate representation of the energy distribution and thus the temperature of the system. This approach can also offer undergraduate students a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of specific heat capacity and its relationship with the energy distribution and temperature. A discussion is presented on the circumstances under which the average occupation number approach can lead to the average energy of the system being inaccurate, with an emphasis on presenting graphical means of the energy distribution and the resulting temperature versus the specific heat

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The general approach employed here can be applied to other orbital triplets in crystal structures. The associated Python code is publicly available online. The transition from $t_{2g}$ only to $e_g$ only behavior across varying interaction strengths and electron filling factors is also examined. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also clarifies the relationship between absolute and relative quantum cohomology through the use of proper rational functions. The findings presented in this paper were previously established in the research of N. Koehl and A. Obuse, but are included here for the sake of completeness. The paper also includes an appendix that discusses the related mathematical concept of toric complete intersections through illustrative diagrams. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our work in the field is progressive, and we invite the medical community to collaborate with us in the hopes of developing a more sophisticated and realistic model that can replicate a wide range of medical conditions and symptoms accurately. This could ultimately lead to a groundbreaking technique for data augmentation and artificial intelligence training with more diversified and representative patterns, and perhaps even a novel approach for point-to-set classification, all while exploring the vast potential of GAN-based editing in the healthcare field. Our code has been made public on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/chexfill. The conference presentation mentioned can be found at https://mi-nips20.github.io/workshops/mim/abstract.html#Towards. The dataset we created, along with the code and guidelines for filling in chest X-rays, are available at https://www.ghru.net/chexfill/. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application includes a user-friendly
graphical interface and is designed for novice and experienced users alike.
ViDaExpert is specifically tailored for problem-solving in various fields like
life sciences, physics, engineering, and social studies. The application is
available for use on Windows, Linux, and Mac operating systems. The core
algorithm code can be accessed under the BSD license, enabling users to
modify the code to suit their specific needs. The ViDaExpert application can
